meta.title: Who really said "When you've exhausted all possibilities, remember this: you haven't"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Thomas Edison, who died in 1931. The line is Robert H. Schuller's, printed in his 1983 book Tough Times Never Last, But Tough People Do!
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When you've exhausted all possibilities, remember this: you haven't'?
meta.ogDescription: Edison died in 1931; this line first appears in 1981, credited to a name Quote Investigator reads as televangelist Robert H. Schuller, who printed it in his 1983 book. QI calls the Edison credit unsupported.

answer.label: Not Thomas Edison — actually Robert H. Schuller
answer.sourceLine: The line is a Robert H. Schuller aphorism, printed on page 27 of his 1983 bestseller Tough Times Never Last, But Tough People Do! and credited in print as early as September 1981 to a “Dr. Robert Shuler” — which Quote Investigator reads as a misspelling of Schuller. Thomas Edison died in 1931 — half a century before the saying’s first known appearance — and Quote Investigator finds the Edison ascription unsupported ↗; it appears to begin with a single Indiana newspaper in 2000.

source.excerpt: When you’ve exhausted all possibilities, remember this: You haven’t!
trail: 1977 — A different saying with the same opening phrase appears in Arthur Bloch’s Murphy’s Law and Other Reasons Why Things Go Wrong!, page 36: a joke about the overlooked obvious solution, not an exhortation to persist, per Quote Investigator ↗.

9 September 1981 — The earliest documented appearance of the saying itself: Helen Peikin’s column in Orlando’s Sentinel Star, page 22, printing it as “When you have exhausted all possibilities, remember this . . . you haven’t” and crediting “Dr. Robert Shuler” — which Quote Investigator conjectures is a misspelling of Schuller ↗.

1983 — Schuller prints it on page 27 of Tough Times Never Last, But Tough People Do!, without crediting anyone else; Wikiquote points to the same book as the location of the line ↗. He reuses it in his 1984 collection Dare To Succeed, page 17.
19 April 2000 — The Reporter-Times of Martinsville, Indiana moves the credit to Thomas Edison, and other newspapers follow; QI calls the shift inexplicable and the Edison attribution unsupported ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording as printed in Schuller’s 1983 book, per Quote Investigator ↗. The 1981 newspaper version reads “When you have exhausted all possibilities, remember this . . . you haven’t.” The circulating Edison version drops the contraction and swaps the colon for a dash. No fuller surrounding passage is reproduced in the sources consulted here — the line stands alone as an aphorism.

source.rightsHolder: Schuller’s estate and his publisher, Thomas Nelson — presumed, not established by any cited source
source.rightsNote: The work containing this line, Tough Times Never Last, But Tough People Do!, was first published in 1983 by Thomas Nelson — listed as Schuller’s notable work ↗ — and is therefore still under US copyright; it will not enter the public domain for decades. Note that the Edison misattribution is what makes this line feel free to use: had Edison written it, the work would long since be public domain. He didn’t, and it isn’t. Quoting a single aphorism with attribution is ordinary fair use; reproducing the surrounding text is not.

author.name: Robert H. Schuller
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Robert H. Schuller
author.bio: Robert Harold Schuller was an American Reformed Church in America minister who founded the Garden Grove Community Church in 1955 and built it into the Crystal Cathedral in Garden Grove, California. From 1970 until his retirement in 2006 he hosted the weekly television broadcast Hour of Power, one of the most-watched religious programs in the United States. His trademark was the compact, quotable one-liner — his 1983 bestseller Tough Times Never Last, But Tough People Do! is built out of them, which is exactly why his aphorisms travelled so easily away from his name.

misattribution.heading: How Edison got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook famous-name migration: a living author’s one-liner detaches from him, drifts for two decades, and lands on a dead inventor whose brand is perseverance.

items.why: Edison died in 1931. The saying is not documented anywhere in his lifetime, and Wikiquote notes it is “not located in Edison’s writings” ↗, filing it under Disputed. Quote Investigator states the ascription is unsupported ↗.

QI identifies this item as the point where the credit inexplicably moved off Schuller and onto Edison ↗, printing it as “When you have exhausted all possibilities, remember this—you haven’t.” Other newspapers followed.

items.who: The Edison Innovation Foundation and Goodreads
items.why: The foundation’s own quotes page lists the line as Edison’s ↗ with no citation for it or any other quote it prints. Goodreads does the same ↗ under a disclaimer that its quotes are community-added and unverified. An Edison-branded source repeating a claim is not evidence for it.

QI records a 1977 precursor ↗ — “Once you have exhausted all possibilities and fail, there will be one solution, simple and obvious, highly visible to everyone else” — which shares the opening phrase but makes the opposite point. It is not the source of Schuller’s line, and it is not Edison’s either.

misattribution.truthLine: Credit belongs to Robert H. Schuller: printed under his own name in 1983, and credited as early as September 1981 under a spelling Quote Investigator reads as his, per Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Edison
lead: The saying is a piece of pure 1980s American motivational rhetoric — a paradox you can fit on a poster. Robert Schuller built a career on exactly this: compact, self-contained one-liners, delivered weekly to a television audience of millions and packaged into bestsellers. When Leslie Hanscom reviewed Tough Times Never Last, But Tough People Do! for Newsday in July 1983, the book’s reliance on such one-liners was the point of the critique — and this line was the specimen he reprinted, quoting page 27 in full as an example of the habit he was needling, according to Quote Investigator’s survey of the record ↗.

A detachable line needs a famous owner, and Edison is the patron saint of not-quitting. He already carries “I have not failed. I’ve just found 10,000 ways that won’t work” and “Our greatest weakness lies in giving up.” A quip about refusing to accept that the possibilities are exhausted slots into that persona without friction — which is precisely what makes the misattribution frictionless, and precisely why it deserves checking rather than nodding at.
context.detailsSummary: The fifty-year gap, in one line
detailsBody: Edison died on 18 October 1931. The earliest documented appearance of this saying that Quote Investigator located ↗ is a column by Helen Peikin in Orlando’s Sentinel Star on 9 September 1981 — where it is already credited to a “Dr. Robert Shuler”, which Quote Investigator conjectures is a misspelling of Schuller, not to Edison.

A related but distinct saying appears earlier, in Arthur Bloch’s 1977 Murphy’s Law and Other Reasons Why Things Go Wrong!: “Once you have exhausted all possibilities and fail, there will be one solution, simple and obvious, highly visible to everyone else.” That is a joke about oversight, not an exhortation about persistence — a cousin of Schuller’s line, not its source, and it is not credited to Edison either.
context.pull: Edison died in 1931. The line first surfaces in 1981.
